Introduction — the fly that closed a continent

blocks.x: Tsetse flies are bloodsucking flies of the genus Glossina. They occur only in tropical Africa, and they are the vectors of African trypanosomiasis in both humans and animals.

items: Sleeping sickness is fatal if untreated.
It occurs in Africa south of the Sahara.
20,000–25,000 people die each year.
Unusually, both sexes of tsetse take blood — unlike mosquitoes and sandflies, where only the female bites. Every tsetse fly is therefore a potential vector.

sections.title: Recognising a tsetse, and knowing the groups

items: Robust flies, 6–15 mm in length.
Distinguished from other biting flies by their forward-pointing mouthparts (proboscis) and characteristic wing venation — the "hatchet cell".
At rest the wings are folded completely over one another like scissors, unlike most flies.
About 30 known species of the genus Glossina.
Austenia — the G. fusca group (forest species)
Nemorhina — the G. palpalis group (riverine/lakeside species)
Glossina — the G. morsitans group (savannah species)

blocks.x: Only nine species and subspecies, belonging to either the G. palpalis or the G. morsitans group, are known to transmit sleeping sickness. So of thirty species, only nine matter medically — and the fusca group is not among them.

sections.title: A fly that gives birth to live young

blocks.x: This is the most distinctive life cycle in medical entomology. The tsetse does not lay batches of eggs. She produces one larva at a time, nourished inside her own uterus by "milk glands" — a strategy called adenotrophic viviparityReproduction in which a single larva is retained and fed inside the mother by specialised milk glands, then deposited fully grown, ready to pupate..

items: A female tsetse mates just once, and is fertile for life from that single insemination (though she may mate again).
After 7–9 days she produces a single egg, which is transported to the uterus and develops into a larva there.
The larva hatches within the uterus after about 4 days and is fed by milk glands. It moults twice and grows to fill most of the mother's abdomen.
About nine days after ovulation, the mother deposits a third-instar larva on the ground. Larvae are 3–8.5 mm long with two black knobs at the posterior end.
The larva burrows 1.5–2 cm underground, forms a puparium and pupates.
The mother continues producing a single larva at roughly nine-day intervals (7–11 days) for her entire life.
The adult emerges from the pupa after about 30 days. Over 12–14 days it matures, mates, and if female deposits its first larva.
Therefore about 50 days elapse between the emergence of one female and the emergence of the first of her offspring.

blocks.x: Why this matters for control: a fly that produces one offspring every nine days has an extremely low reproductive rate. That is a weakness — and it is precisely why the sterile insect technique works so well against tsetse.

items: Caused by Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (and T. b. rhodesiense).
Note that T. brucei brucei does not infect humans — it is an animal parasite.
Trypanosoma congolense — the most prevalent species affecting cattle and small ruminants.
T. vivax
T. brucei brucei
Trypanosoma simiae — causes a particularly virulent disease in pigs.

blocks.x: How the parasite develops — the two-host cycle

items: The tsetse takes a blood meal and injects metacyclic trypomastigotes — the infective stage.
These become bloodstream trypomastigotes and are carried around the body.
They multiply by binary fission in body fluids — blood, lymph and spinal fluid.
Another tsetse ingests bloodstream trypomastigotes, which become procyclic trypomastigotes in the midgut and multiply.
These leave the midgut and become epimastigotes.
Epimastigotes multiply in the salivary gland and transform into metacyclic trypomastigotes — completing the loop.
Cattle and possibly wild ungulates are reservoirs for T. b. rhodesiense.

sections.title: Signs and symptoms of sleeping sickness

blocks.x: Read the disease in two stages: first the parasite is in the blood and lymph, then it crosses into the nervous system. The name of the disease comes only from the second stage.

items: The lymph glands near the bite often become swollen — this is the earliest sign.
Spleen enlargement, oedema, and endocrine disorders such as sterility
Impotence, and abortion in women
Sleeplessness, aimless scratching of the skin, and a transient rash
Hepatomegaly, some digestive disturbance, and some myocardial symptoms

blocks.x: Nervous system involvement — <term d="Inflammation of the brain and its coverings — the late stage of sleeping sickness.">meningoencephalitis</term>

items: Trembling and inability to speak properly
Progressive mental dullness and apathy
Excessive sleeping — the feature that names the disease
Incontinence
Rapid weight loss, continuing irregular fever
Oedema of the limbs and inability to walk without help
If untreated, coma develops, leading finally to death

blocks.x: Notice the paradox worth remembering: the patient has sleeplessness early and excessive sleeping late — the sleep cycle is inverted, not simply increased.

items: Insecticide-treated tsetse traps.
Odour-baited insecticide-treated targets/screens — tsetse are strongly attracted to host odours such as carbon dioxide and acetone.
Insecticide on livestock by spraying, dipping or pour-on — the cattle become the bait.
Ground spraying of insecticide on resting and breeding sites.
Aerial spraying.

Sterile insect technique — releasing sterilised males, used especially in the eradication phase. It works because the female mates only once: if that mating is with a sterile male, she is barren for life.
Clearing bush around homesteads, to remove resting sites.

blocks.x: Biting midges are the smallest man-biting insects. They are famous less for the disease they carry than for being an intolerable biting nuisance — too small to see, and they attack in swarms.

items: Order: Diptera · Sub-order: Nematocera
Family: Ceratopogonidae
Genera: Culicoides, Leptoconops, Lasiohelea
Species of note: C. milnei, C. grahamii
Biting nuisance — crepuscular (active at dusk and dawn), biting people such as campers, fishermen, hunters and gardeners, as well as pets, livestock and wildlife.
Filariasis.
Size: 1.5–3 mm — the smallest man-biting insect, hence the nickname "no-see-um".
Build: robust, with short legs.

Head: small, with bead-like, many-segmented antennae (15 segments) — the many-segmented antenna is the mark of the sub-order Nematocera. Antennae are plumose (feathery, in males) or pilose (hairy, in females). Prominent eyes.
Mouthparts: inconspicuous and dagger-like, resembling those of the black fly.
Thorax: bears humeral pits — a diagnostic feature.
Wings: short and broad, with dark and white patches, and crossed over the body at rest. The patterned wing is how Culicoides species are identified.
Abdomen: 9 segments; dull grey, yellowish, brown or black. Males show prominent claspers.
Females bite exposed parts of the body — man, mammals and birds.
Adults also feed on sugar solutions for energy.
Basically crepuscular insects, and exophilic (they prefer to rest and feed outdoors) — which is why indoor spraying works poorly against them.

blocks.x: Biting midges are holometabolous — complete metamorphosis. The larva is the stage to recognise: a white, eel-like, structureless worm with a striking serpentine swimming motion.

items: Small and ovoid, about 0.5 mm, black or brown, banana-shaped.
Laid on wet soil and rank moist vegetation, tree holes, banana stumps, marshy areas and decaying leaf litter.
Laid in batches of 30–250–450.
Hatch in 2–9 days, depending on species and temperature.
Cylindrical, white and long — they resemble an eel (worm-like).
Black, conical, cylindrical head.
12 visible, similar segments (3 thoracic + 9 abdominal).
No hairs or bristles — devoid of any surface structure.
Two four-lobed retractile gills on the terminal abdominal segment.
Scavengers, with a characteristic serpentine movement.
Found in aquatic, semi-aquatic and moist soil habitats: tree holes, marshy/boggy/swampy areas, horse and cow manure.
Four larval instars; some species have a proleg to aid movement.
Development takes 14–25 days. The larvae are very difficult to find — which is precisely why larval control fails.
Resembles a mosquito pupa.
Two prominent segmented breathing trumpets.
Unsegmented cephalothorax.
Prominent horn-like processes on the last abdominal segment.
Found in the drier areas of the habitat — unlike the mosquito pupa, which stays in water.
Pupal period: 3–10 days.
Very active just before 7 pm.
Bites cause intense itching and welts that persist a long time — an allergic reaction, not damage from the bite itself.
They move in swarms ("no-see-ums").
A genuine threat to the tourist industry, especially in Europe and the Americas.
Dipetalonema perstans — causes dermatitis; East Africa.
Dipetalonema streptocerca — West Africa, common in the rainforest areas of Ghana, Nigeria and Cameroon; transmitted by C. grahamii.

blocks.x: The <term d="The larval stage of filarial worms found in blood or skin.">microfilariae</term>

items: Non-periodic — they can be found in the blood at any time of day, unlike Wuchereria, which is nocturnally periodic. This matters practically: you can take the blood sample whenever you like.
Non-pathogenic.
Moult twice in the thoracic muscles of the vector.
Cause morbidity and allergic reactions in man rather than severe disease.

blocks.x: Several viral and protozoan diseases of domestic and wild animals and poultry are attributed to biting midges — for example equine encephalitis in sheep and horses. Their veterinary importance far exceeds their human importance.

sections.title: Why biting midges are so hard to control

blocks.x: The core problem is stated plainly in the lecture: their habitats are diffuse and extensive, so reducing them is laborious and impractical.

items: Breeding habitats include fresh and salt water marshes and wet coastlands — vast areas, not discrete containers.
Land may have to be drained or filled in, changing water flow patterns — expensive and environmentally costly.
Organochlorines such as dieldrin and DDT have been used.
Personal protection — repellents, and screens on windows or patios. Screens must be small mesh, because ordinary mesh lets a 1.5 mm midge straight through.
Removal trapping and insecticide-treated targets using carbon dioxide as an attractant.

blocks.x: Compare with mosquitoes: mosquito larvae sit in identifiable pools and containers that can be treated, but midge larvae are spread thinly through marsh and manure across whole landscapes.
